paragraphs: A³T investigates how pretraining can help models generate speech. The paper starts from a gap: learning speech representations had improved tasks that interpret audio, while its potential for speech synthesis remained less developed. Producing high-quality speech requires representations that support reconstruction of acoustic detail as well as understanding.

The training task hides portions of the acoustic signal and asks the model to reconstruct them. It supplies both text and acoustic-text alignment, giving the model information about which parts of the audio correspond to which parts of the text. This makes the relationship between spoken content and acoustic structure explicit during pretraining.

The resulting model produces reconstructed spectrograms that can be used directly for speech editing and text-to-speech generation for unseen speakers. The reported experiments show better speech editing performance than the compared state-of-the-art models, along with improved multi-speaker synthesis without an external speaker verification model. These findings support reconstruction with alignment information as a useful pretraining approach for speech generation.
icml-2022-a-3-t-alignment-aware-acoustic.tldr: A³T learns to reconstruct masked audio using text and alignment information, improving speech editing and multi-speaker synthesis.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to measure similarity between graphs whose vertices lack attributes. Its central concern is structural correspondence: a comparison should account for which vertices occupy corresponding locations across graphs. Merely comparing collections of graph components can miss this information, a shortcoming the authors identify in many existing graph kernels.

The proposed Hierarchical Transitive-Aligned Kernel aligns vertices through a hierarchy of prototype graphs. These prototypes provide a shared basis for correspondence across the graphs being compared. The construction guarantees transitivity of the correspondence information, addressing a property that most existing matching kernels do not provide.

The kernel also incorporates information from the entire collection of graphs under comparison, allowing the similarity calculation to capture characteristics beyond an isolated graph pair. The paper presents these properties as three theoretical advantages: structural correspondence, transitive alignment, and richer collection-wide information. Experimental evaluations support the kernel’s effectiveness. The contribution is therefore both a particular similarity measure and a structured way to make graph alignments consistent.
icml-2022-a-hierarchical-transitive-alig.tldr: A graph kernel uses hierarchical prototypes to incorporate consistent vertex correspondences and information from all graphs being compared.

paragraphs: Neural network watermarks are intended to preserve evidence of a model creator’s ownership when someone copies or modifies the model. The paper addresses a weakness in evaluating these watermarks solely through attacks: resistance to the attacks already tested can disappear when an adversary uses a new strategy or tunes an existing one more effectively.

The authors propose a watermarking method with a mathematical certificate based on randomized smoothing. Their guarantee concerns the size of changes to the model’s parameters. A watermark cannot be removed unless those parameters move by more than a specified threshold measured using the ℓ2 norm.

This threshold gives a precise scope to the guarantee: it certifies resistance within a bounded region of parameter changes. Exceeding the threshold is necessary for removal under the certificate, but is not itself a promise that removal will succeed. Alongside this theoretical result, the authors report stronger empirical robustness than previous watermarking methods. The contribution combines attack evaluations with a quantified guarantee about changes a successful removal must require.
icml-2022-certified-neural-network-water.tldr: Randomized smoothing certifies that a neural network watermark survives parameter changes within a specified ℓ2 threshold.

paragraphs: This paper examines how neural machine translation improves as the amount of training data grows, and whether architecture or data quality changes that relationship. For encoder-decoder Transformers, the authors establish a power-law relationship between test loss and training sample count, with an additional dependence on model size.

They then vary the learning setup systematically. Architecture comparisons include a Transformer-LSTM hybrid and a decoder-only Transformer trained with a language modeling loss. Data-quality experiments include filtering and adding independent, identically distributed synthetic noise. Across these changes, the estimated data-scaling exponents change only slightly.

That result suggests that, in the studied settings, adding data can compensate for marginally worse architectures or training data. It does not imply that every data source supports the same improvement rate. The authors find a contrasting result when back-translated data replaces parallel data: the scaling exponent can degrade substantially. The distinction matters because data quantity and data source can affect the scaling relationship differently, even when several other changes leave its exponent largely intact.
icml-2022-data-scaling-laws-in-nmt-the-e.tldr: Translation scaling exponents change little under several architecture and noise variations, but can worsen substantially with back-translated data.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning uses the data itself to provide a training signal, but its practical objectives often differ across speech, vision, and language. Data2vec asks whether the same learning method can work in all three areas. Its contribution is a shared training framework that can be applied to each of these modalities.

Using a standard Transformer, the method learns from an input with some portions masked. Its target is a latent representation computed from the complete input in a self-distillation setup. Because that target incorporates context from the full input, predicting it asks the model to recover information beyond an isolated word, visual token, or speech unit.

This choice makes contextual representations the common prediction target across modalities. The reported experiments cover speech recognition, image classification, and natural language understanding, reaching either a new state of the art or performance competitive with predominant approaches. The findings support the usefulness of a common self-supervised objective across these tasks, while retaining the abstract’s distinction between leading and competitive results.
icml-2022-data2vec-a-general-framework-f.tldr: Data2vec uses one self-supervised learning method across speech, vision, and language by predicting contextual representations from masked inputs.

paragraphs: The paper studies causal inference from observational data when a treatment can take a continuous range of values. The target is a causal response curve describing how outcomes respond across that range. The authors focus particularly on treatment values that appear infrequently in the observed data, where estimating that curve is challenging.

Their algorithm builds on entropy balancing, a framework for assigning weights to observations. The new step is to learn those weights through end-to-end optimization that directly targets causal inference accuracy. The weights can be adapted to different datasets and causal inference algorithms, making their construction responsive to the estimation procedure they support.

The paper also develops a consistency theory for entropy balancing with continuous treatments. This provides a theoretical component alongside the algorithm’s direct optimization of accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show improved causal inference accuracy compared with entropy balancing. Together, these contributions connect the choice of observation weights to the downstream causal estimation task, including the challenge posed by sparsely observed treatment values.
icml-2022-end-to-end-balancing-for-causa.tldr: End-to-end entropy balancing learns observation weights to improve causal response estimation for continuous treatments.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate data through an iterative process, making generation across all timesteps computationally expensive. This paper studies covariance design as a way to improve generation when only a subset of timesteps is used. Covariance is a consequential modeling choice because it shapes the uncertainty represented during the generation process.

The authors derive optimal diagonal and full covariance expressions, then develop corrections for cases where the model’s mean is imperfect. They express both the optimal covariance and its correction through conditional expectations of functions of noise. This decomposition turns covariance estimation into learning those conditional expectations, explicitly accounting for errors in the mean.

The approach applies to diffusion models with discrete or continuous timesteps. For computational efficiency, the implementation uses diagonal covariance, parameter sharing, and two-stage training. Experiments report better likelihood results than a wide range of covariance designs and improved sample quality, particularly with few timesteps. The findings emphasize that covariance estimation and mean accuracy should be considered together when improving the quality of shorter diffusion generation procedures.
icml-2022-estimating-the-optimal-covaria.tldr: Learning covariance estimates that account for imperfect means improves diffusion likelihoods and sample quality, especially with few generation steps.

paragraphs: This paper studies federated learning problems that combine a smooth, data-dependent loss with a nonsmooth regularizer. Examples include sparse regression with Lasso and low-rank matrix recovery with nuclear norm regularization. The aim is to understand both how quickly distributed optimization proceeds and how accurately it recovers the underlying statistical structure.

For strongly convex and smooth losses, the authors introduce Fast Federated Dual Averaging. They prove fast convergence, linear speedup, and fewer communication rounds in the composite setting. These results address the need to coordinate many devices while communicating infrequently, with guarantees covering both iterations and communication.

A second algorithm, Multi-stage Federated Dual Averaging, handles losses with restricted strong convexity and smoothness. Its high-probability complexity guarantee provides linear speedup up to optimal statistical precision. The distinction between the two algorithms matters because their guarantees use different curvature conditions and address different aspects of recovery. Experiments on synthetic and real data show better performance than the compared baselines, complementing the paper’s optimization and statistical guarantees.
icml-2022-fast-composite-optimization-an.tldr: Two federated dual-averaging algorithms provide fast composite optimization and statistical recovery guarantees under their respective curvature conditions.

paragraphs: The paper extends fictitious play, a decentralized learning procedure for repeatedly playing a static game, to discounted stochastic games. This move introduces a dynamic setting in which the game evolves over time. The central question is whether the resulting learning procedures approach stationary Nash equilibria in the game classes studied.

For identical-interest discounted stochastic games, the authors prove that a family of discrete-time fictitious-play procedures converges to the set of stationary Nash equilibria. They also study continuous-time counterparts, including a previously introduced best-response dynamic as a special case. Their continuous-time convergence results cover both identical-interest and zero-sum discounted stochastic games.

The connection between continuous and discrete time is another part of the contribution. Using stochastic approximation, the authors derive some discrete-time convergence results from the continuous-time analysis, including results for zero-sum and team stochastic games. These findings extend equilibrium-learning guarantees beyond static games. Their scope remains tied to the specified game structures, and convergence to an equilibrium set does not assert a unique equilibrium.
icml-2022-fictitious-play-and-best-respo.tldr: Extended fictitious-play and best-response procedures have stationary-equilibrium convergence guarantees in specified classes of discounted stochastic games.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can lead a classifier to fit labeling errors and generalize poorly. Many approaches address this during classifier training, which creates a practical problem when the classifier is already trained and its training process is unavailable. This paper studies a separate correction step applied to the classifier’s predictions.

Noisy Prediction Calibration, or NPC, introduces a new kind of transition matrix and estimates it through a generative model. That matrix supports converting noisy predictions into estimates of the true labels. The method operates as post-processing, so its correction does not require participation in the original classifier learning procedure.

The authors prove a theoretical alignment with transition-matrix-based methods and report that NPC provides a more accurate route to estimating true labels empirically. It improves every evaluated baseline on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Its stated applicability includes classifiers trained with noisy-label methods, provided the training instances and their predictions are available. This requirement distinguishes avoiding classifier retraining from avoiding access to the training examples altogether.
icml-2022-from-noisy-prediction-to-true-.tldr: NPC uses a generative transition model to correct predictions after training, improving all evaluated noisy-label classifiers.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification allows a single example to have several labels, making relationships among labels useful for prediction. This paper introduces C-GMVAE, a Gaussian mixture variational autoencoder combined with supervised contrastive learning. The model learns representations of both input features and labels, aligning their latent spaces.

The contrastive objective uses available label information to learn embeddings that capture label correlations. The authors present this as a way to obtain meaningful relationships through learning, where many existing methods add complex neural modules for that purpose. The Gaussian mixture prior supplies multiple modes in the latent space and is intended to alleviate posterior collapse and excessive regularization associated with unimodal approaches.

Across multiple public datasets, C-GMVAE outperforms existing methods. It can often match other models’ full performance using only half of the training data, an empirical result rather than a universal data requirement. The learned embeddings also offer insight into interactions between labels. Together, the findings connect predictive performance, data efficiency, and interpretation to the model’s combined representation-learning design.
icml-2022-gaussian-mixture-variational-a.tldr: C-GMVAE combines supervised contrastive learning and a Gaussian mixture latent space to improve multi-label prediction and capture label relationships.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a generative model can support several visual perception tasks through shared representations. Its focus extends beyond making realistic images: the generated content should help a multi-task learning system perform its tasks. The authors propose multi-task oriented generative modeling, or MGM, to pursue that objective.

MGM couples a discriminative multi-task network with a generative network. A central challenge is that synthesizing images together with pixel-level annotations for multiple tasks is difficult. The framework instead makes use of generated images paired with weak annotations, specifically image-level scene labels, to assist multiple visual tasks.

Experiments on NYUv2 and Taskonomy report large improvements across all evaluated tasks and consistent gains over state-of-the-art multi-task approaches at different sample sizes. These results support the usefulness of a shared generative component for multi-task perception. The role of weak annotations is especially consequential: the framework can extract benefits from synthesized examples without requiring those examples to carry the full pixel-level annotation set for the multiple tasks.
icml-2022-generative-modeling-for-multi-.tldr: MGM couples generative and multi-task networks so synthesized images with scene labels improve multiple visual perception tasks.

paragraphs: Imitation learning often combines demonstrations from people or agents whose abilities differ across situations. Treating them as equally capable can cause a learned policy to absorb each demonstrator’s weaknesses. This paper models expertise as something to infer, allowing the usefulness of a demonstrator’s behavior to vary with the state.

The authors jointly optimize a policy and estimates of demonstrator expertise without requiring expertise supervision. This joint model is designed to learn from each demonstrator’s optimal behavior while filtering out suboptimal behavior. It also estimates a demonstrator’s expertise at a given state, making the expertise model useful beyond producing the final policy.

Combining strong behavior from different demonstrators can yield a single policy that outperforms even the best individual demonstrator. The reported evaluation includes Robomimic robotic control tasks, MiniGrid, and chess. The method beats competing approaches in 21 of 23 settings, with an average final-reward improvement of 7% and improvements reaching 60%. These results support accounting for state-dependent expertise when learning from mixed-quality demonstrations.
icml-2022-imitation-learning-by-estimati.tldr: Jointly learning a policy and demonstrators’ state-dependent expertise helps imitation learning combine strengths and filter weak behavior.

paragraphs: Strategic learning studies how individuals respond to decision rules, such as those used in loan approvals or admissions. This paper removes the common assumption that people know the rule. Instead, individuals infer it from peers, creating subpopulations with different kinds and amounts of information about how decisions are made.

The authors show that these information differences can have consequential equilibrium effects. A decision rule chosen to optimize welfare across subpopulations may still cause some groups’ true quality to decline. This is a possible negative externality of the overall optimization, rather than a claim that every opaque decision rule harms some group.

The analysis also identifies positive possibilities. In many natural cases, optimal improvement can be guaranteed for all subpopulations simultaneously. An information overlap proxy helps characterize disparities in improvement, and a stated natural condition permits improvements for every group while preserving high predictive accuracy. Experiments on real-world datasets complement the theory. The paper thus connects access to information about a rule with both behavioral improvement and disparities across groups.
icml-2022-information-discrepancy-in-str.tldr: Unequal knowledge of decision rules can produce harmful group-level effects, while suitable conditions allow improvement for every group.

paragraphs: Input-label pairs may not contain enough information to distinguish stable predictive features from spurious ones. This paper explores how related tasks can provide additional guidance. Its starting observation is that tasks often share similar biases, so information about unstable features in a source task may help train a more robust target classifier.

The method first contrasts different data environments in the source task to learn a representation that encodes unstable features. It then uses that representation to cluster examples in the target task. Training minimizes the worst-case risk across these clusters, directing attention to performance across the groups created by the transferred representation.

The distinctive transfer is therefore knowledge of instability: the source task helps expose divisions relevant to robust target training. Evaluations on text and image classification show that the method maintains target-task robustness in both synthetically generated and real-world environments. These results support using shared bias information across related tasks, while the motivation depends on the relevance of source-task instabilities to the target setting.
icml-2022-learning-stable-classifiers-by.tldr: Transferring representations of unstable source-task features helps organize target data for robust worst-case training.

paragraphs: Continuous normalizing flows generate distributions by evolving an initial distribution through an ordinary differential equation. This paper develops a training objective for these models on manifolds. Instead of focusing only on the final distribution, it compares the model’s evolving density with a target sequence of densities connecting noise and data.

The proposed probability path divergence uses a logarithmic mass-conservation equation linking target log probabilities to the flow’s vector field. Its practical benefit is that training does not require solving an ordinary differential equation at every iteration. The formulation accommodates manifold data and a broad family of target paths that connect noise to data in finite time.

The authors prove that probability path divergence bounds classical probability divergences, giving the objective a theoretical connection to distribution matching. Experiments achieve state-of-the-art likelihood and sample-quality results on existing low-dimensional manifold benchmarks. They also demonstrate scaling to moderately high-dimensional manifolds, presented as the first such generative-model example. These results support the training formulation’s usefulness beyond the low-dimensional settings used in established benchmarks.
icml-2022-matching-normalizing-flows-and.tldr: Probability path divergence trains continuous normalizing flows on manifolds without solving an ODE at each training iteration.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning in sequential games where players have incomplete information and receive bandit feedback from play. Its main goal is to find an approximate Nash equilibrium efficiently in two-player zero-sum games. The relevant resource is the number of episodes needed to reach a requested approximation accuracy.

The authors introduce Balanced Online Mirror Descent and Balanced Counterfactual Regret Minimization. Both integrate balanced exploration policies into established learning procedures. Their episode requirement scales with (XA + YB)/ε², up to logarithmic factors, where X and Y count the players’ information sets and A and B count their actions.

Previous best-known dependence involved X²A + Y²B, so the new algorithms substantially improve how sample requirements grow with information sets. The resulting bound matches the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors, which is the basis for calling the algorithms near-optimal. The paper also extends its results to learning coarse correlated equilibria in multiplayer general-sum games, where the equilibrium target differs from the two-player zero-sum result.
icml-2022-near-optimal-learning-of-exten.tldr: Balanced exploration yields near-optimal episode complexity for learning approximate Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games.

paragraphs: Fisher’s Linear Discriminant Analysis seeks a lower-dimensional representation that separates classes while keeping examples within each class close together. This paper extends that discrimination objective to a neural network embedding. The proposed Neural Fisher Discriminant Analysis retains the original criterion while allowing a two-layer network to perform the mapping.

The central technical step is to transform the optimal neural embedding problem into a convex optimization problem. The authors use tools from convex optimization to obtain a formulation that can be interpreted and solved to global optimality. Thus, the contribution concerns both the representation objective and a way to optimize the specified network embedding.

Global optimality here refers to the paper’s discrimination criterion for its two-layer embedding problem. It gives a precise meaning to an optimal representation within that formulation. The authors evaluate the method on synthetic and real datasets, although the abstract does not state a comparative performance outcome. The main stated result is the connection between neural discriminant embeddings and a tractable convex formulation.
icml-2022-neural-fisher-discriminant-ana.tldr: Neural Fisher Discriminant Analysis reformulates optimal two-layer discriminant embeddings as a convex problem solvable to global optimality.

paragraphs: Inverse kinematics finds joint parameters that place selected parts of a joint chain at desired positions. Several joint configurations can satisfy the same positional target, so a useful method must account for multiple solutions while responding quickly. This paper builds a neural method around the hierarchical structure of the chain.

A hypernetwork produces the parameters of a separate primary network for each joint. Each primary network outputs a distribution over possible joint angles, conditioned on the desired position and the angles already sampled for earlier joints. Sequential sampling therefore represents dependencies along the chain rather than choosing each joint angle independently.

The hypernetwork can be trained using available matching pairs of joint angles and positions without observing multiple solutions for each target. At test time, sequential sampling yields a joint distribution with high variance, supporting a range of configurations. The authors demonstrate advantages over other inverse-kinematics methods both for individual target instances and for following an end-effector path in Cartesian space. These evaluations address isolated solutions as well as movement along a desired path.
icml-2022-neural-inverse-kinematic-5a7a2.tldr: A hypernetwork learns sequential joint-angle distributions to generate multiple inverse-kinematics solutions from ordinary angle-position training pairs.

paragraphs: This paper examines a hidden issue in convergence analysis for policy search with continuous actions. Analyses commonly assume that a policy’s score function is bounded, but even Gaussian policies violate that assumption. Introducing an exploration tolerance to describe a bounded region creates a persistent bias in the expected policy-gradient-norm attenuation rate.

Heavy-tailed policy parameterizations can have bounded score functions and thus mitigate this source of bias. However, they can also make algorithmic updates unstable. The authors study policy-gradient convergence under these parameterizations and propose combining mirror-ascent-type updates with gradient tracking to stabilize learning.

Their main theoretical result establishes convergence with constant batch sizes. This supports a training regime that does not require the batch size to grow without bound. In experiments, the scheme with a heavy-tailed policy accumulates more reward than standard benchmarks across several settings. The contribution connects three issues that otherwise appear separately: the validity of score-function assumptions, bias introduced by restricting exploration, and stable optimization under heavy-tailed policies.
icml-2022-on-the-hidden-biases-of-policy.tldr: Mirror-ascent updates with gradient tracking stabilize heavy-tailed policy learning and provide convergence with constant batch sizes.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning brings representations of semantically related examples closer while distinguishing them from negative samples. This paper studies why increasing the number of negatives can help downstream classification. Earlier theoretical bounds covered only limited negative-sample counts and could be too large to provide a useful account of the observed behavior.

The authors derive upper and lower bounds connecting downstream classification loss with contrastive loss for all negative-sample sizes. Their analysis uses a simplified setting in which positive pairs come from the true distribution, rather than being created through data augmentation. That assumption defines the setting in which the theoretical connection is established.

The bounds suggest that contrastive loss serves as a surrogate for supervised loss, with a shrinking gap as the negative-sample count grows. This gives a theoretical explanation for improvements associated with larger negative sets in earlier empirical studies. Experiments on synthetic, vision, and language datasets are consistent with the analysis. The result clarifies the relationship between the objectives without making an unconditional claim about every practical contrastive-learning pipeline.
icml-2022-on-the-surrogate-gap-between-c.tldr: Under a simplified positive-pair assumption, new bounds explain larger negative sets through a shrinking contrastive-to-supervised surrogate gap.

paragraphs: Two models can represent the same examples in different spaces, making direct comparison challenging. This paper introduces Representation Topology Divergence, or RTD, to compare the multiscale topology of two representations. It treats each representation as a point cloud and measures differences in their structural organization across scales.

The method requires equal-sized point clouds with a one-to-one correspondence between points. This matches the setting where each example has one representation in each space. The ambient spaces themselves can differ, so the comparison does not require both representations to occupy the same surrounding coordinate space.

Experiments show agreement between RTD and intuitive judgments of representation similarity, as well as sensitivity to fine topological structure. The authors use it to investigate training dynamics, distribution shift, transfer learning, ensembles, and disentanglement in vision and natural language processing. Its contribution is a practical topological perspective on representation comparison across these problems. RTD measures a particular structural aspect of similarity, consistent with the paper’s recognition that comparing representations is a problem with multiple aspects.
icml-2022-representation-topology-diverg.tldr: RTD compares the multiscale topology of corresponding data representations, even when they occupy different ambient spaces.

paragraphs: The paper studies data generated by two sparse linear regression models when the source model for each observation is unknown. Solving the problem requires recovering both regression parameter vectors and assigning observations to the correct model. The original formulation is NP-hard, and commonly used methods such as expectation-maximization can become trapped at local minima.

The authors introduce an invex relaxation with theoretical recovery guarantees. Their formulation uses a carefully constructed primal-dual witness framework. The stated results include exact recovery of the observation labels and close approximations to the two regression parameter vectors, addressing the assignment and estimation parts of the problem together.

The recovered parameter vectors also match the true vectors in support and sign: they identify the same nonzero coordinates and the same directions of their coefficients. This is more specific than a claim of numerical closeness alone. The paper further shows sample complexity with only logarithmic dependence on parameter dimension. These guarantees describe the proposed formulation’s recovery results rather than a claim that arbitrary NP-hard regression instances become easy.
icml-2022-sparse-mixed-linear-regression.tldr: An invex relaxation provides exact label recovery and accurate sparse parameter recovery for a two-component mixed linear regression problem.

paragraphs: This paper studies generalization guarantees for noisy stochastic learning algorithms through stability. It bounds generalization error using expected stability rather than uniform stability, aiming for quantitatively sharper results. The distinction shifts the analysis toward expected behavior instead of requiring the same stability control uniformly.

The main framework, Exponential Family Langevin Dynamics, generalizes stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics and includes noisy forms of Sign-SGD and quantized SGD. For this family, the authors establish data-dependent generalization bounds with a 1/n sample dependence. The bounds depend on gradient discrepancy rather than gradient norms, providing a different way to quantify the sensitivity relevant to generalization.

The authors also prove optimization guarantees for special cases of the framework, keeping that result distinct from the broader generalization analysis. Benchmark experiments show that the bounds are non-vacuous, sharper than existing bounds, and behave appropriately under noisy labels. Together, the contributions expand the algorithms covered by stability analysis and make its estimates more informative in the evaluated settings, connecting a broader theoretical framework with empirical bound quality.
icml-2022-stability-based-generalization.tldr: Expected-stability analysis yields sharper data-dependent generalization bounds for a broad family of noisy optimization algorithms.

paragraphs: In contextual dueling bandits, a learner selects two alternatives each round and observes a noisy preference between them. This paper assumes that feedback follows a linear stochastic transitivity model with context-dependent utilities, called CoLST. The learner’s objective is to include the alternative with the highest latent utility in the selected pair.

The proposed CoLSTIM algorithm imitates the feedback process using perturbed estimates of the alternatives’ contextual utilities. This provides a computationally efficient selection rule within the assumed model. When each alternative has a d-dimensional feature vector, the authors prove regret growing on the order of √(dT), up to logarithmic factors, over T rounds.

The paper also establishes a lower bound for weak regret that refines existing average-regret analysis and supports the algorithm’s optimality claim. This matters because the objective concerns whether the best alternative appears in the duel. Experiments show better performance than state-of-the-art algorithms for special cases of CoLST models. The theoretical and empirical conclusions are therefore anchored to the specified preference-model setting.
icml-2022-stochastic-contextual-dueling-.tldr: CoLSTIM efficiently chooses contextual duels using perturbed utility estimates and achieves near-optimal regret under the CoLST feedback model.
